# Case Study: Building an Enterprise Agent Platform {#sec-capstone}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** This chapter has no measurement of its own. It is a
worked example — a system constructed so that the book's own measurements bear
on it — rather than a report on a particular company's deployment. Measurements
from earlier chapters are combined below with explicit workload assumptions, and
each measurement is cited to its chapter; nothing here is a new claim about the
world. Read it as an exercise in assembling what you already
have, which is also what the capstone asks of you.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- trace one system from requirements through architecture to production,
  naming the chapter behind each decision;
- write an architecture decision record that includes the rejected
  alternatives;
- build a cost, latency and risk budget for a system before you build the
  system;
- anticipate the failures that appear at the second team and the tenth agent;
- scope and deliver the capstone project.

## The system, and the four things it will not do {#sec-capstone-requirements}

The example is a support platform for a mid-size Turkish e-commerce company.
Agents answer customer questions about orders, shipping and returns, in Turkish,
over roughly 40,000 conversations a month. Three tools: look up an order, check
a shipment, open a return request. A return request can be cancelled; the
refund payment is not an agent tool — the agent can only propose one, and the
refund service decides. Escalation to a human is always available.

The requirements that shape everything:

| requirement | where it bites |
|:--|:--|
| Turkish, including the morphology that breaks naive tokenisation | @sec-turkish-nlp, and every eval set below |
| Customer messages contain national IDs, IBANs and addresses | @sec-guardrails, @sec-governance |
| A return is money leaving the company | @sec-guardrails' reversibility taxonomy |
| Answers must be traceable to a policy document | @sec-rag, @sec-observability |
| One platform team, five product teams wanting agents | @sec-capstone-platform |

: What the requirements actually constrain {tbl-colwidths="[46,54]"}

[The non-goals are worth more than the goals, and they should be written
first.]{.hl} This system will not: generate marketing copy, answer questions
outside orders, shipping and returns, let an agent take any action a human cannot
undo within one working day — money moves only through the refund service, under
its ceiling and approval rule — or operate without a human escalation path. Each of those is a
decision that removes an entire class of failure — and each will be argued
against by someone who wants one more feature, which is why they are written
down before anyone is invested.

## Seven decisions, and what was rejected {#sec-capstone-decisions}

An architecture decision record is worth writing only if it records the
alternative honestly. The compressed form — and note that one row below is not
a technical decision at all, which is the point of putting it in the same
table:

| decision | chosen | rejected, and why |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Model access** | one gateway in front of all providers | direct SDK calls per service — cheaper to start, and then attribution, pinning and rate limits have five implementations (@sec-gateway) |
| **Where the loop lives** | durable execution with checkpointed state | in-memory loop behind a request handler — fine until a deploy lands mid-conversation (@sec-deployment) |
| **Retrieval** | hybrid search over the policy corpus, with citations | full-context stuffing of all policies — simpler, and @sec-serving's prefill cost makes it the dominant latency term. Note the alternative this row does *not* reject: BM25 or dense retrieval alone, which @sec-retrieval found beating unweighted rank fusion on its corpus. Measure the single retrievers before assuming the hybrid |
| **PII** | detect and tokenise reversibly at the boundary | mask destructively — safe and it breaks order lookup (@sec-guardrails) |
| **Refunds** | agent proposes, service enforces the ceiling, human approves above it | agent calls the refund API with a limit in the prompt — a limit in a prompt is a request (@sec-agent-security) |
| **Eval** | golden set in the repo, gate on every prompt change | manual spot-checks before release — @sec-production-eval measured what slips through |
| **Where the provider sits** | a Türkiye-region deployment where one exists, otherwise a standard contract under KVKK Article 9 | "the gateway abstracts it away" — the gateway centralises the choice, it does not make it a technical one (@sec-governance-kvkk) |

: Seven decisions; the rejected column is the one to read
{tbl-colwidths="[16,34,50]"}

Two of these deserve their reasoning spelled out, because they are the ones
teams most often get backwards.

**Retrieval rather than long context.** Stuffing every policy document into the
prompt is genuinely simpler and it loses on the numbers: @sec-serving measured
91.0% of wall-clock time spent before the first character at 7,427 tokens of
context, and decode slowing from 189 to 141 tokens per second as the window
filled. Long context is charged twice. Retrieval adds a component and removes
the dominant latency term.

**The refund ceiling lives in the refund service.** This is the single most
important line in the design, and @sec-agent-security is why: an agent that
reads customer messages is reading attacker-controlled input, and a planted
instruction made an agent call a tool it was never asked to call on **25 runs out
of 25**. If the ceiling is in the prompt, the ceiling is a suggestion.

## The first agent, chapter by chapter {#sec-capstone-first}

The path from notebook to production, with the chapter that governs each step:

1. **Write the task down as an eval before writing the agent** (@sec-llm-eval).
   Fifty real conversations, labelled by what a good answer would have been.
2. **Build the retrieval layer and measure it alone** (@sec-retrieval,
   @sec-rag). If the right policy document is not in the top five, no amount of
   prompting fixes the answer.
3. **Write the tools as APIs, not as prompts** (@sec-tool-design), each with its
   reversibility class attached (@sec-guardrails).
4. **Build the smallest loop that works** (@sec-agent-anatomy), with all three
   ceilings set from the start (@sec-deployment).
5. **Add structured output and validate it** (@sec-decoding) — the validator is
   also the escalation signal in @sec-capstone-budget.
6. **Instrument before you have a problem** (@sec-observability), including
   conversation id, both model fields, token counts and your own dimensions.
7. **Gate the prompt on the eval suite** (@sec-production-eval), with a threshold
   set from a measured noise floor rather than a round number.
8. **Attack it yourself before shipping** (@sec-agent-security), and write down
   the rate.

Steps 1 and 8 are the ones teams skip, and they are the two that decide whether
the rest was worth doing.

## What the book's numbers say this costs {#sec-capstone-budget}

The useful discipline before building is a budget assembled from measurements
you already have. Every figure below is quoted from an earlier chapter, and the
arithmetic is the only new thing.

Read the whole section as a **starting estimate, not a validated budget for this
platform**. Each number came from a different model, a different corpus and a
different task, and several transfer badly: the PII precision belongs to Turkish
support text with this book's identifier mix, and the attack and detection rates
belong to one model with one prompt and one attack set. Treat them as the
assumptions to write down and then measure first, which is what the closing
sentence of this section is about.

**Latency.** @sec-serving's split — prefill around 2,000 tokens per second
against decode at 190 — means a token you *write* takes about eleven times as
long as a token you *read*, on that hardware. Which half dominates is therefore a question about your own
ratio rather than a universal fact, and the ratio changes as soon as you make
the retrieval decision. At 7,427 in and 64 out, the request @sec-serving
reports as 91% prefill, decode is 8%. At the shape planned for below — a
thousand tokens of context and a two-sentence Turkish answer, call it 150
tokens — prefill is 0.50 s and decode is 0.79 s, so **decode is the larger
term**, and time-to-first-token stops being the thing to optimise. That is a
consequence of the design, not an argument against it.

Prompt caching still goes first, because it is free of quality risk: warm
prefill measured **flat at 12–16 ms regardless of prompt length**. But scale
the multiplier to your own prefill share rather than carrying the headline. The
9.0× @sec-serving reports is at 4,247 tokens; at a thousand tokens of context
and a 150-token answer the same lever is about **1.6×** on the whole request.
Quote the mechanism, recompute the number.

**Token volume.** @sec-summarization's measurement — **890 prompt tokens
against 53 generated** — is one shape to plan for, and worth converting before
using: at eleven-to-one, those 53 output tokens are worth about 583 input ones
against a prompt of 890, so [sending less saves more than writing less, but
"almost nothing" overstates it]{.hl}. At
40,000 conversations a month with a few model calls each, the boilerplate in
your system prompt is a larger line item than the model you chose.

**Telemetry.** @sec-observability measured **4.8 spans and 3,167 bytes per run**
on 301-token prompts, of which **48.3% was prompt and completion text** — and at
890-token prompts the same structure is **6,163 bytes with 73.4% content**. A
run there is one agent invocation with its model and tool calls, and a
conversation can hold several, so write the volume with *r*, the average runs
per conversation: 40,000 × *r* runs a month. At *r* = 1 that is roughly 190,000
spans and, with content recorded at that prompt size, about **0.25 GB**; on the
measured 301-token prompts it is 0.13 GB. Multiply both by *r*; small either way. At a million runs it is 6 GB, and the decision to
record content is a near-fourfold difference. Decide it deliberately, and sample
content while keeping it on every error.

**Evaluation.** @sec-llm-eval's sizing says 100 items resolves a 13.4-point
difference and 1,000 resolves 4.8 — so a hundred-item golden set finds broken,
not better. A gate that compares runs on the same items is what makes small
regressions visible anyway. @sec-production-eval measured a run-to-run `sd` of
**0.26 points** (range 0.60) and used a 1-point threshold, about 4 × `sd`; in its
resampling that gave **4.3% false blocks** at 100 items and caught a
review-invisible prompt regression **99.4%** of the time. Those rates illustrate
how the threshold behaves rather than measure a paired gate — the per-item
pairings were not stored — so measure your own gate before relying on them.

**Guardrails.** @sec-guardrails' detector numbers set the escalation rate: an
eleven-digit pattern alone is **40% precise**, and pattern plus checksum-or-context
reaches **99.1% precision at 93.6% recall**. The residual matters — roughly one
in fifteen real identifiers is not caught by the union, which is a number to put
in the DPIA rather than to hide.

**Security.** @sec-agent-security's attack success of **92–100%** against an
agent with an outward tool, and a detection rate of **14.7%** for the one
detector prompt with a usable false-positive rate, on the three attack framings
that were demonstrated to work — not a general "best case" — is why the
architecture separates the agent that reads tickets from the one that can move
money. That is not a mitigation with a residual rate; it is a pair that has been
broken — provided the handoff between them is a validated structured payload
rather than free text the second agent reads as instruction, and the refund
service authorises against the user rather than against whatever the first agent
asked for. Two processes alone are not the boundary; the data contract is.

**Routing.** @sec-classification measured an LLM's verbalised confidence as a
detector of its own errors at **AUROC 0.667**, against 0.843 for a fine-tuned
classifier's own probability on the same task — real signal, and not enough to
route on blindly. The version of routing that survives
is the cascade of @sec-governance: answer with the small model, escalate on a
validator failure rather than on a predicted difficulty.

[Notice what the budget did not require: a single new experiment.]{.hl} Eight
chapters of measurement, assembled, produce a design with numbers attached — and
the places where the numbers are missing are exactly where your first
measurements should go.

## The second team and the tenth agent {#sec-capstone-platform}

Everything above is one agent. The failures that appear later are organisational,
and they arrive on a schedule.

**At the second team**, the shared thing is prompts and tools, and the first
platform failure is a tool changed by one team breaking another team's agent. The
fix is the one from software: tools are versioned interfaces with owners
(@sec-tool-design), and a tool definition change is reviewed like a dependency
bump (@sec-agent-security).

**At the fifth agent**, nobody can answer "how many agents do we run and what can
they reach". An **agent registry** — one row per agent, listing its tools, its
data access, its owner and its reversibility profile — is unglamorous and is the
artefact every audit, incident and cost review will need (@sec-governance).

**At the tenth agent**, the platform team becomes the bottleneck, and the
resolution is a golden path rather than a review queue: a template repository
where the eval gate, tracing, PII boundary and tool classification are already
wired, so the compliant way is the fastest way. [A platform team that reviews
everything scales linearly and then stops; one that makes the safe path the easy
path does not.]{.hl}

**Throughout**, cost attribution has to exist from the first agent, because
@sec-observability's dimensions are expensive to add retrospectively — you can
join them in later only if some other durable record kept them, and nothing
recovers what was never written down — and the number a budget review wants is
cost per resolved ticket, not cost per session.

## What breaks {#sec-capstone-retro}

The honest retrospective, written as the failures this book's measurements
predict rather than as war stories. Each is a plausible failure mode to test for
and plan around.

**The eval set will be too small and too easy.** It starts as fifty cases
someone wrote in an afternoon, it gets easier as you fix what is in it, and its
flat score will be read as stability. @sec-production-eval: a set that has not
changed in six months is stale, and it still produces a green check.

**Someone will edit a prompt without running the gate**, because the change is
obviously cosmetic. @sec-production-eval measured a pure reordering costing 3.40
points of field accuracy — nearly six times the noise floor — with the entire
regression inside one field.

**The PII detector will be tuned on recall and break the product.** At 40%
precision it masks the order numbers agents need, and the response will be to
turn it off rather than to fix precision (@sec-guardrails).

**The first serious incident will be an approval queue nobody rejects
anything in.** A 99% approval rate alone does not show it — a well-targeted gate
should approve almost everything. Planted errors do: if reviewers approve items
known to be wrong, the queue is a delay wearing oversight's clothes, and nobody
sees it until someone runs that check (@sec-guardrails).

**Someone will propose giving the ticket-reading agent the refund tool** to
remove a hop. The answer is in @sec-agent-security, and it needs to be a
measurement — your own attack success rate — rather than an argument.

**Choosing a provider is a legal decision before it is a latency one.** This is
a Turkish company handling TCKN and IBAN, so a US-hosted provider is a transfer
abroad under KVKK Article 9, and @sec-governance-kvkk has the consequence: the
Board has issued no adequacy decision, so the route is the published standard
contract with its five-business-day notification. If the company is a bank, a
payment institution or an insurer, the sectoral rule cuts above that and the
question may not be open at all. One gateway in front of all providers helps
here — it is the single place where that choice is recorded and enforced — but
it does not make the choice, and a design review that skips this is not a design
review.

**The model will be upgraded underneath you.** @sec-gateway's alias problem: if
you record only the requested model, you find out weeks later from a quality
regression. Two attributes do not prevent the upgrade — pinning the version
does — but they are what lets you *detect and investigate* it the same day
(@sec-observability).

What would be done differently, in one line: **write the eval and the attack
before writing the agent.** Both are cheap at the start and neither gets written
once the system works.

## The capstone project {#sec-capstone-project}

Your capstone is the small version of this chapter: one agent, at least one real
tool, an eval harness shipped alongside it, and a written argument for the
decisions you made.

The brief, deliverables, rubric and timeline are in @sec-capstone-brief. What is
worth saying here is what distinguishes the projects that go well:

- **They scope down early.** One task done properly beats three demonstrated.
  The non-goals list is the first artefact, not the last.
- **They measure something.** A project with one honest number — including a
  negative result — is stronger than one with a polished demo, and this book has
  spent the preceding thirty-eight chapters making that case.
- **They report what did not work.** @sec-llm-eval's asymmetry applies to
  coursework too: a bad number gets investigated and a good one gets published.
  Say what you tried that failed.
- **They separate the claim from the evidence.** "Our agent resolves 80% of
  tickets" needs a set, a definition of resolved, and an interval.

Non-CS students are graded on reasoning, not on code elegance. A clear argument
about why an approach was chosen, with a measurement that could have refuted it,
is the deliverable.

## Intuition checks {#sec-capstone-intuition}

Answer each before opening it. These are synthesis questions: each pulls
together two or three chapters, which is what the capstone will ask of you.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Long context or retrieval, for a policy-grounded support agent?

Retrieval, and the reason is latency arithmetic rather than taste.

@sec-serving measured **91.0%** of wall-clock time elapsing before the first
character at 7,427 tokens of context, and decode falling from **189 to 141
tokens per second** as the window filled. Long context is charged twice: once in
prefill, then again on every generated token.

Stuffing all policies in is simpler and makes the dominant latency term as large
as possible. Retrieval adds a component you must evaluate separately (@sec-retrieval)
and removes that term — plus it gives you citations, which the
requirement asked for anyway.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Where does the refund ceiling live?

In the refund service, enforced in code.

An agent that reads customer messages reads attacker-controlled input, and
@sec-agent-security measured a planted instruction making an agent call an
outward tool on **25 runs out of 25**, with a hidden-in-markup variant working
**23 of 25**. A ceiling written in the prompt is a request to a component the
attacker also gets to write to.

The stronger move is structural: do not give the ticket-reading agent the refund
tool at all. That breaks the pair rather than mitigating it, and the cost —
an extra hop — is the cheapest security you will buy all year.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your golden set has 100 items. What can it tell you?

That something is broken, not that something is better.

@sec-llm-eval's sizing: at 80% power on an 80%-accurate system, 100 items
resolves a **13.4-point** difference and 1,000 resolves **4.8**. Most real
improvements are 2–5 points, so a hundred-item set cannot see the thing it was
built to see — as an unpaired comparison.

But a gate compares two runs on the *same* items, and in @sec-production-eval's
resampling a 1-point threshold on 100 items caught a 3.4-point regression
**99.4%** of the time. That rate takes the observed drop as the true effect and
could not match items across prompts, so it illustrates the threshold rather
than measuring a paired gate. Same set, different question: use it as a gate,
not as evidence that version B is better than version A in the population.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. What do you build before the agent?

The eval and the attack.

Both are cheap before anything works and neither gets written afterwards. The
eval gives you a definition of done and the gate that protects it
(@sec-production-eval); the attack gives you a number for the risk you are
carrying (@sec-agent-security), which is the only form in which that risk
survives a conversation with a stakeholder.

Everything else — retrieval, tools, the loop, tracing — is buildable in any
order. These two are not, because after the system works the incentive to write
them disappears.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Five teams want agents. What does the platform team build?

A golden path, not a review queue.

Reviewing every agent scales linearly with the number of teams and then stops.
A template repository with the eval gate, tracing, PII boundary and tool
classification already wired makes the compliant way the fastest way, which is
the only version of governance that survives contact with a deadline.

Plus one artefact nobody wants to own: an **agent registry** — one row per agent
with its tools, data access, owner and reversibility profile. Every audit,
incident and cost review needs it, and reconstructing it after the fact depends on
whatever other records happen to survive — the same limit as
@sec-observability's cost dimensions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your dashboard is green, the gate is passing, users are unhappy. Where do you look?

At what each instrument cannot see, in order.

The gate is green about **your suite**, which is a claim about coverage — go to
traces, find the complained-about runs, and check whether the failure class
exists in the set at all (@sec-production-eval). The dashboard is green about
**transport**: @sec-observability's point is that a `status=OK` span happily
contains a confidently wrong answer.

Then rule out the boring cause before the interesting ones: a change within the
observed run-to-run range needs more evidence — more runs, a paired comparison —
before you attribute it to the intervention. @sec-production-eval measured a run-to-run
`sd` of **0.26 points** and a five-run *range* of **0.60**; the range is what a
single new run is compared against, and the `sd` is what a gate threshold is
built from. Say which you are quoting.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-capstone-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions below
recur in the two credible open sources this book uses throughout. This chapter's
answers are syntheses of measurements made earlier in the book.
:::

### Testing whether you can design a system

**Q: Design a customer support agent for a Turkish e-commerce company.**

Start with non-goals, because they remove failure classes: no agent action that
cannot be undone within a working day, no scope outside orders, shipping and
returns, always a human escalation path. Then the shape — retrieval over policy documents rather
than long context, for the latency reason; a gateway for attribution and
pinning; durable state so a deploy mid-conversation is survivable; PII tokenised
reversibly at the boundary so lookups still work; and the refund ceiling
enforced in the refund service, with the ticket-reading agent not holding that
tool at all.

**Q: What would you measure before building it?**

Nothing new, at first — assemble what is known. Prefill-versus-decode to find
which half your latency is in; prompt and completion token counts, because you
pay for reading rather than writing; spans and bytes per run before turning
content logging on; the eval-set size your target improvement requires; your PII
detector's precision as well as recall; and your own attack success rate. Where
the assembled budget has a hole is where the first experiment goes.

**Q: How do you decide whether to use a smaller model?**

Not from a benchmark table. Make it a measurement on your own suite, and prefer
a cascade to a routing decision: answer with the small model and escalate on a
runtime validity check, because a validator is a signal you actually have at
request time, where predicted difficulty is a guess — @sec-classification
measured verbalised confidence as a detector of a model's own errors at AUROC
0.667, against 0.843 for a real probability, which is real signal and not enough
to route on blindly.

### Testing whether you have run a platform

**Q: Five teams want to build agents. What do you centralise?**

The choke point and the golden path. One gateway for attribution, pinning and
limits; a template repository with the eval gate, tracing, PII boundary and tool
classification pre-wired; and an agent registry listing every agent's tools, data
access and owner. Do not centralise review — a platform team that reviews
everything is a bottleneck by construction. Make the safe path the fast path
instead.

**Q: What is the first thing that breaks at scale, organisationally?**

A tool changed by one team breaking another team's agent, because tool
definitions are shared context and nobody treated them as an interface. Version
them, give them owners, and review changes as dependency bumps. Shortly after
that: nobody can answer what agents exist and what they can reach, which is the
registry's job, and which is only as reconstructable later as the other records
that happen to survive.

**Q: Your agent platform's costs tripled. How do you find out why?**

Only if you recorded the dimensions in advance — user, team, feature,
environment, and the outcome — because you cannot group by what you did not
record. Then check the usual order: content logging turned on somewhere,
retries amplifying a degradation, prompt growth pushing you off the cache's
byte-identical prefix, or a loop hitting no ceiling. Report cost per resolved
ticket rather than per session, or a feature nobody completes will look cheap.

## Lab: build the budget before the system {#sec-capstone-lab}

### Step 1 — write the non-goals

Four to six sentences saying what your capstone will not do. Circulate them. Any
disagreement surfaces now, when changing them is free.

### Step 2 — write the eval before the agent

Fifty real cases with what a good answer would be. Note how long it took; that
number is the honest cost of knowing whether your system works.

### Step 3 — assemble the budget from this book's numbers

Latency, token volume, telemetry bytes, eval-set size, guardrail precision,
attack success. Cite each to its chapter. Where you cannot fill a cell, that is
your first experiment — write down what it would take to measure it.

### Step 4 — write three ADRs with the rejected alternative

Decision, alternatives, consequences. The rejected column must contain a real
argument, not a straw man. If you cannot argue the other side, you have not
finished thinking about the decision.

### Step 5 — classify your tools and enforce one limit outside the model

Every tool into @sec-guardrails' reversibility classes, then one numeric or
allowlist limit in the tool's implementation, with a test proving a persuasive
prompt cannot move it.

### Step 6 — attack your own system and record the rate

Four payload framings, twenty-five runs each, with a clean control
(@sec-agent-security). Put the number in your report whatever it says.

### Step 7 — measure your gate's noise floor and set a threshold

Five identical runs; record the run-to-run `sd` as well as the widest gap, and
set the threshold at roughly 4 × `sd` rather than just above the range
(@sec-production-eval). Then measure the false-block rate on enough no-op
changes to resolve it: zero blocks in five still leaves a 95% Wilson upper bound
of 43%.

### What to hand in

Your non-goals; the eval set with the time it took; the budget table with every
cell cited or marked as a gap; three ADRs; the tool classification with one
enforced limit and its test; your attack success rates with the clean control;
and your measured noise floor with the threshold you chose and its measured
false-block rate.

## Exercises {#sec-capstone-exercises}

1. **The ADR you will be asked about.** Write the record for the most
   consequential decision in your capstone, including the alternative you
   rejected and the argument for it that you found hardest to dismiss.

2. **The 100× cost model.** Produce the cost model for your system at a hundred
   times its traffic. Name what breaks first, and whether it is money, latency,
   or someone's attention.

3. **The budget with holes.** Build the budget table of
   @sec-capstone-budget for your own system. Report how many cells you could
   fill from this book, how many from your own measurements, and how many are
   still guesses.

4. **Break one pair.** Find one agent in your design that reads untrusted
   content and holds an outward tool. Split it, and report what capability you
   lost (@sec-agent-security).

5. **The registry.** Write the agent registry for a system you run — tools, data
   access, owner, reversibility profile. Report what you could not answer without
   asking someone.

6. **The golden path.** Take the compliance requirements for a new agent at your
   organisation and design the template that satisfies them by default. Then
   estimate how long the non-template path takes, in days.

7. **The retrospective in advance.** Write the postmortem for the incident you
   think is most likely in your system, before it happens. Then implement the one
   control that would have prevented it.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-capstone-deeper}

Before reading: try to write your system's budget table from memory. The cells
you cannot fill are the chapters to reread.

This chapter cites no new sources — it assembles the book's own. The table below
is a reading order rather than a bibliography.

| if you are stuck on | reread |
|:--|:--|
| what to measure before building | @sec-llm-eval and @sec-agent-eval, then @sec-production-eval for the gate |
| whether the latency is the prompt or the answer | @sec-serving, and the prefill/decode split specifically |
| where a limit should live | @sec-guardrails for the taxonomy, @sec-agent-security for why the prompt is not a place |
| why quality moved and nothing changed | @sec-production-eval on noise floors, @sec-observability on the responded model |
| what your obligations are | @sec-governance, and note the dates move |
| how to make the safe path the fast one | @sec-capstone-platform above, and @sec-gateway for the choke point |

: A reading order for the capstone {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

## What to remember {#sec-capstone-summary}

- **Write the non-goals first.** Each one removes a class of failure, and each
  will be argued against later by someone who wants one more feature. Deciding
  them before anyone is invested is the cheapest architectural work you will do.

- **An ADR without a real rejected alternative is a press release.** If you
  cannot argue the other side, the decision has not been made yet.

- **You can budget a system before you build it, from measurements you already
  have.** Latency from @sec-serving's prefill/decode split, token volume from
  **890 prompt tokens against 53 generated**, telemetry from **4.8 spans and
  3,167 bytes per run**, eval size from @sec-llm-eval's **13.4 points at 100
  items**, guardrail precision from **40% pattern-only**, and risk from
  @sec-agent-security's **92–100%** attack success. [Where the budget has a hole
  is where your first experiment goes.]{.hl}

- **Retrieval beats long context on arithmetic, not taste.** @sec-serving
  measured **91.0%** of the wall clock elapsing before the first character at
  7,427 tokens, and decode falling from **189 to 141 tokens per second**.

- **Every limit that matters is enforced outside the model.** A ceiling in a
  prompt is a request, and the stronger move is not to give the untrusted-input
  agent the dangerous tool at all — breaking the pair rather than mitigating it.

- **Write the eval and the attack before the agent.** Both are cheap at the
  start, neither gets written once the system works, and they are the two things
  that decide whether the rest was worth building.

- **The platform failures arrive on a schedule.** At the second team, a shared
  tool breaks someone; at the fifth agent, nobody knows what exists; at the
  tenth, the platform team is the bottleneck. Versioned tools with owners, an
  agent registry, and a golden path — in that order.

- **A platform team that reviews everything scales linearly and then stops.**
  Make the compliant path the fastest path instead, because that is the only
  governance that survives a deadline.

- **Report the claim with its evidence.** "Resolves 80% of tickets" needs a set,
  a definition of resolved, and an interval. That standard is what this book has
  been arguing for since @sec-llm-eval, and it is what the capstone is graded
  on.
